Jahath
jā'hath
n. (a recurring Levitical name: a son of Libni in the line of Gershom, an Izharite chief, and an overseer of the workmen in Josiah's repair of the temple)
From Hebrew Yachath, of uncertain derivation, possibly connected with a root meaning to snatch up or take hold. Four or five Levites of the name appear in Chronicles.

Biblical Definition

Jahath is a name that belongs entirely to the tribe of Levi. He stands in the Gershomite line in the Chronicler's genealogy of the singers — “Of Gershom; Libni his son, Jahath his son, Zimmah his son” (1Ch 6:20) — the ancestry that runs down to Asaph, who stood at David's right hand with cymbals. A Jahath heads a Shimeite house among the Levites David numbered (1Ch 23:10), and another is an Izharite: “Of the Izharites; Shelomoth: of the sons of Shelomoth; Jahath” (1Ch 24:22). The most memorable bearer appears at the end of the kingdom of Judah. When Josiah, having found the book of the law, set men to repair the house of the LORD, the record singles out the supervisors and the manner of the work in one sentence: “And the men did the work faithfully: and the overseers of them were Jahath and Obadiah, the Levites, of the sons of Merari; and Zechariah and Meshullam, of the sons of the Kohathites, to set it forward; and other of the Levites, all that could skill of instruments of musick” (2Ch 34:12). Levites overseeing carpenters, and musicians among them — the trades and the singers on the same site, with a Levite over both.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Jahath; in sacred history it is the name of several Levites, chiefly an overseer of the workmen in the repair of the temple under Josiah.

expand to see more

JAHATH, n. A Levite of the line of Gershom, the son of Libni.

The name occurs also among the sons of Shimei in the courses of David.

An Izharite of the name is reckoned in the genealogy of the sons of Kohath.

Jahath, of the sons of Merari, was an overseer of the workmen when Josiah repaired the house of the LORD.

It is recorded of that work that the men did it faithfully.

1Ch 6:20 — "Of Gershom; Libni his son, Jahath his son, Zimmah his son,"

1Ch 23:10 — "And the sons of Shimei were, Jahath, Zina, and Jeush, and Beriah. These four were the sons of Shimei."

1Ch 24:22 — "Of the Izharites; Shelomoth: of the sons of Shelomoth; Jahath."

2Ch 34:12 — "And the men did the work faithfully: and the overseers of them were Jahath and Obadiah, the Levites, of the sons of Merari; and Zechariah and Meshullam, of the sons of the Kohathites, to set it forward; and other of the Levites, all that could skill of instruments of musick."

Modern Corruption

Josiah's reformation is read as a pious tidying-up or as a late political invention, when Chronicles presents it as a nation recovering a lost book and rebuilding around it.

expand to see more

The critical commonplace is that the law-book found in Josiah's temple was written in Josiah's reign — a reforming party's programme presented as an ancient discovery. The dictionary rejects the reconstruction and holds Mosaic authorship. It is worth noticing what the theory requires: that the king, the high priest, the scribe, the prophetess and the assembled nation were either parties to a forgery or deceived by one, and that the deception produced a reformation whose chief effect was to tell Judah it was under a curse. Frauds are not usually designed to terrify their sponsors. What Chronicles describes is what the text says happened — a book neglected until it was lost in its own house, and a king who tore his clothes when he finally heard it read.

The second and more useful observation is about how reformation actually proceeds. It was not a mood; it was carpenters, masons, timber, hewn stone, and Levites keeping the accounts, of whom Chronicles says twice over that they dealt faithfully. Recovery of the word led directly to repair of the house and to the greatest passover since the days of Samuel. Genuine reform always takes that shape: the word first, then the ordinary obedience that follows it, and men counting money honestly because they have heard God speak. “to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word” (Isa 66:2) is Isaiah's standard, and Josiah's generation met it: “because thine heart was tender, and thou didst humble thyself before God” (2Ch 34:27).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Yachath (H3189), Jahath; Gereshom (H1648), Gershom; paqad (H6485), to oversee, appoint; 'emunah (H530), faithfulness; chazaq (H2388), to repair, strengthen.

expand to see more

Hebrew Yachath (H3189) — Jahath; the name of several Levites in Chronicles.

Hebrew Gereshom (H1648) — Gershom; the Levitical line in which one Jahath stands.

Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, number, appoint as overseer; his office under Josiah.

Hebrew 'emunah (H530) — faithfulness; “the men did the work faithfully”.

Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to strengthen, repair; the word for the work on the house.

Usage

"“Jahath his son, Zimmah his son” — a singer's pedigree running down to Asaph."

"“The overseers of them were Jahath and Obadiah, the Levites” — Levites over carpenters."

"“The men did the work faithfully” — the sentence Chronicles chose to record."
